stem: Two tools exist: analyze_content ("Analyzes content and returns insights"), which is meant for web search results, and analyze_document ("Analyzes documents and returns insights"), which is meant for uploaded PDFs. Across 200 runs the agent sent web search results to analyze_document 47% of the time. What is the most effective remediation?

options.text: Rename analyze_content to extract_web_results and give it a web-specific description with stated inputs and boundaries.
Add eight few-shot examples to the system prompt showing web results routed to analyze_content on every request.
Retire analyze_content and route both web results and documents through analyze_document, which accepts either input.
Add a preprocessing step that tags each input with its source type, and reference the tag in both descriptions.

explanation: The names and descriptions are near-identical, so the model has nothing to select on. Renaming to remove the functional overlap and rewriting the description around inputs and boundaries fixes it where the model reads it.

why.B: Pays tokens on every request to compensate for two descriptions that could simply say what they are for.
why.C: Collapses a real capability distinction instead of expressing it, and the merged tool inherits both contracts.
why.D: Builds preprocessing to work around wording, and the overlapping descriptions still compete once the tag is read.

stem: search_papers and search_archives have overlapping descriptions and the agent picks between them roughly at random. Which three changes attack the cause? (Select 3)

options.text: Rename one tool so the two names no longer describe the same activity.
State in each description which inputs belong to it and which belong to the other.
Audit the system prompt for phrases that name one tool's domain and skew selection.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing the correct routing for recent ambiguous queries.

explanation: Misrouting between similar tools comes from names and descriptions that do not differentiate, and from system prompt wording that can override even good descriptions. Renaming, explicit boundaries and a prompt audit address all three.

why.D: Pays token overhead on every request to compensate for two descriptions that still do not differentiate; the overlap itself is untouched.

stem: A generic analyze_document tool is asked to do three jobs depending on phrasing: pull numeric data points, produce a summary, and check a claim against the text. Output shape varies run to run and downstream parsing breaks. What restructuring is recommended?

options.text: Route requests through a classifier that decides which of the three jobs was intended before the call.
Split it into extract_data_points, summarize_content and verify_claim_against_source, each with its own contract.
Add a required mode parameter with three enum values, and document each mode inside the existing description.
Keep one tool and add few-shot examples for all three jobs, showing the expected output shape for each.

explanation: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools gives each one a precise description and a single predictable output shape, which is what the downstream parser needs.

why.A: Duplicates the selection the model already performs, and the tool still returns three different shapes.
why.C: Better than nothing, but one description still covers three jobs and one response schema still covers three output shapes.
why.D: Examples cannot give a single tool three output contracts; the shape stays whatever the model produces.

stem: Your tool descriptions are detailed and well differentiated, yet the agent calls escalate_to_human on 41% of tickets, including straightforward damage replacements. The system prompt contains the line "When in doubt, involve a human." What is the likely explanation?

options.text: escalate_to_human is declared last in the tools array, and later entries carry more weight in selection.
The other tools return large payloads, so the model avoids them to conserve its context budget.
Keyword-sensitive system prompt wording creates tool associations that override the descriptions.
escalate_to_human has the shortest description, and short descriptions are cheaper for the model to satisfy.

explanation: System prompts can create unintended tool associations. A blanket phrase like this one reads as a standing instruction to reach for the escalation tool, and it competes with descriptions the model would otherwise follow.

why.A: Position in the tools array carries no selection semantics.
why.B: Result size is unknown at selection time and does not produce a consistent bias toward one named tool.
why.D: Description length is not a cost the model optimizes when selecting a tool.

stem: You add an MCP tool search_code_semantic that searches a semantic index of the repository, but the agent keeps reaching for the built-in Grep. Its description reads "Searches the codebase." What is the most effective step?

options.text: Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools so semantic search is the only option left to it.
Rename the MCP tool to grep_semantic so the model associates it with the search it already reaches for.
Add a CLAUDE.md line instructing Claude to prefer search_code_semantic over Grep in this repository.
Expand its description to state what it indexes, what it returns, and when to prefer it over text search.

explanation: Agents fall back to familiar built-in tools when an MCP tool's description does not make its added capability legible. Explaining the capability and the output is what changes the selection.

why.A: Removing a genuinely useful built-in tool to force adoption degrades every other task that needed plain text search.
why.B: A name nudge without saying what the tool can do that Grep cannot.
why.C: Prompt-level preference is weaker and further from the point of selection than the description the model reads with the tool.

stem: get_customer has a 400 word description, but it documents the backend: which tables it reads, its cache layer, and its retry policy. The agent still confuses it with lookup_order. What is wrong with the description?

options.text: It documents how the tool works rather than what it accepts and when to choose it over similar tools.
It is too long, and descriptions past a few hundred words are truncated before the model sees them.
It describes a backend the model cannot reach itself, so the model discounts the description as a whole.
It omits an output schema, which is where the model actually reads a tool's selection criteria.

explanation: Length is not the problem, relevance is. The description is the primary selection signal, so it has to carry inputs, example requests, edge cases and the boundary against similar tools. Implementation detail crowds those out.

why.B: There is no such truncation rule, and a shorter description of the same content would fail the same way.
why.C: The model reads the description as given; it does not discount text about internals, it just cannot select on it.
why.D: An output schema helps, but the missing signal here is the input and boundary information, not the return shape.

stem: You replace a generic fetch_url tool with load_document, which accepts only URLs that resolve to a supported document type and rejects everything else. What problem does this primarily solve?

options.text: It makes the tool safe to hand to every subagent, since it can only ever reach document endpoints.
It constrains the tool to its purpose, so the agent cannot repurpose it for unrelated retrieval.
It shrinks result payloads, since parsed document text is returned instead of arbitrary page content.
It removes the need for structured error responses, since bad URLs are rejected before the call runs.

explanation: A generic retrieval tool invites uses it was never designed for. Replacing it with a constrained alternative that validates its input keeps the tool inside the contract its description promises.

why.A: A narrow purpose is not the same as universal access; which agents hold the tool is a separate distribution decision.
why.C: Some payloads may shrink, but that is a side effect; the same agent could still pull an unrelated document.
why.D: A validating tool needs structured errors more, not less: every rejection has to tell the agent why and whether to retry.

stem: All four of your MCP tools fail the same way: isError true with the text "Operation failed. Please try again." The agent retries permission denials until it hits its cap and abandons transient timeouts after one attempt. What should the tools return alongside isError?

options.text: The raw exception and stack trace, so the agent has every detail the failing service reported.
A retry-after duration in seconds on every failure, so the agent always knows when to try again.
An errorCategory (transient, validation, permission), an isRetryable boolean, and a reason.
An HTTP-style numeric status code in the error text, which the agent maps to a retry decision.

explanation: isError says a call failed; it does not say what kind of failure or whether another attempt could succeed. Category, retryability and a readable reason are the metadata that lets the agent retry the right things and explain the rest.

why.A: Stack traces burn context and leak internals while still never stating whether a retry is worth making.
why.B: A duration implies every failure is worth waiting out, which is exactly wrong for validation and permission errors.
why.D: A bare code requires the agent to know a mapping nobody gave it, and the same code can be transient in one tool and terminal in another.

stem: process_refund rejects a request because the order shipped 47 days ago and the return window is 30 days. What should the tool return so the agent handles it well?

options.text: A transient error, in case the shipping date was stale when the window was computed.
A validation error, since the order failed a constraint the tool checks before refunding.
A success with refund_amount 0 and a note in the response text explaining the refusal.
A business error with retriable: false and a customer-friendly statement of the policy.

explanation: A policy rejection is a business error. Marking it non-retryable stops the agent from burning attempts on a decision that will not change, and the customer-friendly text gives it something accurate to say.

why.A: Retrying a policy decision never succeeds and delays the answer the customer is waiting for.
why.B: The arguments were well formed; policy rejected the request, not the input format, and validation errors invite the agent to reformat and retry.
why.C: Reporting a refusal as a success is silent suppression, and a zero amount reads downstream as a completed refund.

stem: A search subagent queries a document archive successfully and the archive returns zero matching documents for the query. How should this be represented to the coordinator?

options.text: A success carrying an empty result set, clearly distinguished from an access failure.
An error with errorCategory transient, so the coordinator retries the archive later.
An error with isRetryable false, so the coordinator stops querying this archive.
A success carrying one placeholder record stating that the archive held no matches.

explanation: A query that ran correctly and matched nothing is a successful result with zero rows. Keeping it distinct from an access failure is what lets the coordinator tell a gap in the sources from a gap in the coverage.

why.B: Retrying a correct query that legitimately matched nothing wastes calls and never changes the answer.
why.C: Still classifies a success as a failure, which distorts coverage reporting even though the retry decision is right.
why.D: Injecting a synthetic record puts non-source text into the synthesis agent's inputs.

stem: A document analysis subagent hits a transient 503 from its storage backend on one of eight documents. It retries twice, the third attempt succeeds, and all eight documents are analyzed. What should it report to the coordinator?

options.text: A success plus a transient error entry, so the coordinator can retry the affected document.
A success: the transient failure was recovered locally and needs no coordinator action.
A structured error describing the 503, so the coordinator sees every backend fault.
A partial result flagged degraded, since one document needed three attempts to read.

explanation: Subagents recover transient failures locally and propagate only what they cannot resolve. All eight documents were analyzed, so there is nothing for the coordinator to decide.

why.A: There is nothing to retry, and a mixed shape forces the coordinator to branch on a condition that has already cleared.
why.C: Escalating resolved noise makes the failures that do need a decision harder to find.
why.D: The output is not degraded; every document was processed and the retry count does not change the result.

stem: Your document analysis subagent calls fetch_document, which returns a normal tool result whose text reads "503 Service Unavailable from the storage backend" with isError left unset. The synthesis agent quotes that string in the report as if it were document content. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Raise a JSON-RPC protocol error so the failure never reaches the model as a tool result.
Return an empty result so there is nothing to quote, and record the 503 in the server log.
Return the result with isError true, plus the error category and whether it is retryable.
Have the synthesis agent scan tool result text for strings like "503" and "unavailable".

explanation: isError is how a tool tells the agent that the call itself failed. With the flag unset, a failure message is indistinguishable from content, so the model treats it as data.

why.A: Protocol errors are for problems like an unknown tool or malformed arguments; a backend that answered 503 is a tool execution error and belongs in the result.
why.B: Turns a failure into a valid empty result, which is the suppression pattern that produces confidently incomplete reports.
why.D: Text sniffing reimplements a flag the protocol already provides, and it misses every phrasing nobody thought to add.

stem: Your support agent's MCP tools returned the four failures below. Which two would correctly carry isRetryable: false, meaning the identical call cannot succeed on a later attempt? (Select 2)

options.text: A 503 from the payments provider during a partial regional outage.
A validation error from a malformed order ID in the arguments.
A permission error; the agent's credentials lack refund authority.
A gateway timeout while the order service was being redeployed.

explanation: Validation and permission failures cannot change while the inputs and credentials stay the same, so a retry is guaranteed waste. Transient conditions are the opposite case.

why.A: A partial outage resolves without any change to the request, so the call is worth retrying.
why.D: A timeout during a redeploy is the archetypal transient failure and clears on its own.

stem: Your extraction pipeline calls a validate_schema MCP tool. On failure it returns isError true with the text "Validation failed". Your wrapper retries any error three times, and last month 61% of all tool calls were retries of failures that could never have succeeded. What change removes most of that waste?

options.text: Lower the retry limit from three to one, cutting two thirds of the retries across every failure.
Add exponential backoff so retries are spaced out and the pipeline stays inside its call budget.
Collect the failing documents and resubmit them in a single overnight run instead of inline.
Return an isRetryable flag with each error so the wrapper skips attempts that cannot succeed.

explanation: The waste is retrying failures that are terminal by nature. Retryability metadata is what lets the caller tell those apart, so the retries that remain are the ones that can actually succeed.

why.A: Cuts good retries and bad retries alike, so transient failures that would have recovered now fail instead.
why.B: Spacing out a doomed retry does not make it succeed; it only makes the pipeline slower.
why.C: Moves the same doomed retries to a later run, and defers results the pipeline needs now.

stem: Your codebase exploration agent carries 18 tools because "it might need them". Selection accuracy has fallen from 91% to 68% against an earlier version that carried 5. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: A larger decision space degrades selection; scope it to the 4-5 tools the role needs.
The 18 descriptions need rewriting; a well-described tool set of any size selects reliably.
The tool definitions are crowding out the context the agent needs for file contents.
The model tier is too low for an 18-tool set and should be raised before the design changes.

explanation: Selection reliability falls as the number of candidate tools rises, because every call is a harder decision. Scoping each agent to its role is the remedy the drop points to.

why.B: Descriptions matter, but good descriptions do not undo the cost of choosing among 18 candidates.
why.C: Tool definitions are small next to file contents, and the symptom is wrong choices rather than lost context.
why.D: Reframes a design problem as a capability problem, and leaves the same 18-way decision in place.

stem: Your document analysis subagent holds the six web search tools as well as its own three parsing tools. In 30% of runs it issues its own searches instead of analyzing the documents the coordinator handed it, and the final report cites sources the coordinator never routed. What is the fix?

options.text: Give the search subagent the parsing tools too, so either agent can finish a document end to end.
Restrict it to its three parsing tools, so all search stays with the coordinator's search subagent.
Keep the search tools and add a system prompt rule against searching unless a document is missing.
Keep the search tools and have the coordinator validate every cited source after synthesis runs.

explanation: Agents with tools outside their specialization use them. Removing the search tools restores the coordinator's control over which sources enter the pipeline, which is what makes provenance traceable.

why.A: Doubles the over-provisioning instead of removing it, and now both agents can drift outside their role.
why.C: Restraint by instruction is probabilistic, and the tool stays one decision away in every run.
why.D: Reactive and expensive: unvetted sources have already shaped the synthesis by the time they are checked.

stem: Your extraction service must return structured data on every call. You have three document schemas and the type is not known in advance. In 4% of calls the model answers in prose and the downstream parser fails. Which tool_choice setting fits?

options.text: tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_generic"}, forcing one permissive fallback schema.
No tool_choice, with a post-processing step that re-prompts whenever the reply comes back as prose.
tool_choice: "any", which guarantees a tool call while the model picks the schema.
tool_choice: "auto" plus a system prompt line requiring one of the three tools every time.

explanation: "any" is exactly the case of must call a tool, may choose which one: the structure is guaranteed by configuration and the schema choice is still the model's.

why.A: Forcing one schema throws away the schema selection the three document types exist for.
why.B: Pays an extra round trip to detect a failure that one configuration setting prevents outright.
why.D: "auto" leaves a text answer available no matter what the prompt says, so the 4% failure mode survives.

stem: Every document must have extract_metadata run before any enrichment tool, because the enrichment tools need the document type it returns. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Set tool_choice: "any" so a tool is always called, and declare extract_metadata first in the array.
Set tool_choice: "auto" and state the required ordering in the system prompt for every document.
Withhold the enrichment tool definitions until the metadata call returns inside the same request.
Force {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} first, then enrich in follow-up turns.

explanation: Forced tool selection is the only setting that guarantees which tool runs. Ordering after that is handled by structuring the follow-up turns, not by anything inside the first one.

why.A: "any" promises a tool call but not which tool, and position in the tools array carries no ordering semantics.
why.B: Ordering by instruction is probabilistic, and the enrichment tools stay available on the first turn.
why.C: The tool set is fixed for the whole request; you cannot add tools mid-turn in response to a call inside it.

stem: Which three statements about tool_choice are accurate? (Select 3)

options.text: {"type": "tool", "name": "x"}: the model must call tool x specifically.
"auto" plus a system prompt line requiring a tool call is equivalent to "any".
"auto": the model may call a tool or may answer with plain text.
"any": the model must call a tool, and it chooses which one.

explanation: These are the documented semantics: auto leaves the decision open, any guarantees a call without constraining which, and the tool form names the one that must be called.

why.B: "auto" leaves a plain-text answer available whatever the prompt says. Only "any" removes that option at the API level.

stem: A report generation subagent is given the full toolset of every other subagent so it can "fill any gap". What is the most likely production consequence?

options.text: It will work outside its specialization, producing output the coordinator cannot validate.
It will call fewer tools overall, since a larger menu makes the model conservative about acting.
It will exhaust the context window on tool definitions before it can read any of the findings.
It will produce equivalent output more slowly, since each turn now evaluates a larger tool list.

explanation: Agents with tools outside their role tend to use them. The report agent starts sourcing its own material, which both lowers quality and breaks the coordinator's control of what went into the report.

why.B: Models do not become cautious as options grow; they choose anyway, and choose worse.
why.C: Tool definitions are not the dominant context cost next to research findings.
why.D: The output does not stay equivalent; content the coordinator never routed ends up in the report.

stem: 78% of your support tickets need a warranty status check. That data sits behind the fulfillment team's MCP server, which exposes 12 tools including write operations such as reissue_shipment and void_invoice. What access design fits the support agent?

options.text: Reimplement all 12 fulfillment tools in the support server so one server covers both roles.
Expose one scoped check_warranty_status tool and route the remaining fulfillment work elsewhere.
Attach the whole fulfillment server and forbid the write tools in the support agent's system prompt.
Have the support agent escalate every warranty question to a human on the fulfillment team.

explanation: Give the agent exactly what its high-frequency need requires and nothing more. One read-only tool covers 78% of tickets while the write operations stay outside the support agent's reach.

why.A: Duplicates another team's logic and re-exposes the same write operations under new names.
why.C: Adds 12 tools to the decision space and leaves destructive operations one probabilistic instruction away.
why.D: Routes the most common case to a human, which is the opposite of what a resolution target needs.

stem: Your team standardizes on a shared Jira MCP server that every developer must have configured. Where does it go, and how is the API token handled?

options.text: Project-scoped .mcp.json with the token inline, and .mcp.json added to .gitignore.
A CLAUDE.md section telling each developer to add the server and its token themselves.
Project-scoped .mcp.json in the repository, with the token written as ${JIRA_TOKEN}.
User-scoped ~/.claude.json on each machine, with the token written inline in the env block.

explanation: Project scope is what makes a server shared and version-controlled, and ${VAR} expansion lets that file be committed with no credential in it.

why.A: Gitignoring the config defeats the point of sharing it, and the value is still sitting in a file next to the code.
why.B: Manual per-developer setup is exactly the work project scope exists to remove, and nothing keeps the setups consistent.
why.D: User scope is for personal and experimental servers, and it leaves every developer to configure the shared server by hand.

stem: You are trialling an experimental MCP server that only you find useful. The project already ships two shared servers in its committed .mcp.json. What happens when you add yours to ~/.claude.json?

options.text: The user-scoped server replaces the project-scoped pair for your sessions in this repository.
Only the project-scoped servers load, because a committed .mcp.json takes precedence.
Your teammates pick up the experimental server the next time they pull the repository.
All three connect and their tools are available together; teammates get only the two shared ones.

explanation: Tools from every configured server are discovered when the connections are established and are all available to the agent at once. User scope stays on your machine.

why.A: The scopes coexist; neither one suppresses the other.
why.B: A project file does not disable user configuration, and both sets of tools load.
why.C: ~/.claude.json is outside the repository and is never distributed by version control.

stem: Your agents spend several calls per session discovering which issues exist before doing any useful work. The MCP server could publish a browsable catalog of issue summaries. How should that catalog be modelled?

options.text: As an MCP resource, so the catalog is visible without exploratory tool calls.
As an MCP tool named list_issues that returns the whole catalog on the first call.
As a CLAUDE.md section regenerated nightly from the issue tracker and committed.
As an MCP prompt the agent invokes at session start to pull the catalog into context.

explanation: Resources are the mechanism for exposing content catalogs such as issue summaries, documentation hierarchies and database schemas, precisely so the agent can see what exists without calling a tool to find out.

why.B: Still costs a decision and a round trip per session, which is the cost the catalog is meant to remove.
why.C: Loads a growing dataset into context on every session and goes stale between regenerations.
why.D: Prompts are user-invoked interaction templates, not a mechanism for exposing content.

stem: Your team needs Jira integration for standard issue and sprint workflows. A maintained community MCP server already covers them. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Skip MCP and call the Jira REST API through Bash, so there is no server to maintain.
Adopt the community server for the standard workflows it already covers.
Write a custom server so the tool descriptions match your team's vocabulary exactly.
Fork the community server now so you control its release cadence and can patch it.

explanation: For a standard integration the existing server is the cheaper and better-tested path. Custom servers earn their maintenance cost only where the workflow is genuinely specific to your team.

why.A: Gives up the described tool interface the model selects from, leaving the agent to compose API calls in a shell.
why.C: Descriptions can be sharpened without owning an entire server, and vocabulary is not worth a build.
why.D: Takes on maintenance before there is any evidence the upstream server falls short.

stem: Which two statements about MCP server scoping in Claude Code are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: ~/.claude.json is where personal or experimental servers belong.
A project-scoped server must also be declared in user scope before its tools load.
Servers connect one at a time, so only the first server's tools are offered in a session.
.mcp.json at project level is where servers the whole team needs belong.

explanation: Project scope is for shared team tooling and travels with the repository; user scope is for personal and experimental servers and stays on the machine.

why.B: Project-scoped servers load from the project file on their own; no second declaration is involved.
why.C: Every configured server connects, and all of their tools are discovered and available together.

stem: Your committed .mcp.json sets "env": { "GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }. One developer's server fails to start and claude mcp list warns about that variable. The rest of the team is fine. What happened?

options.text: That developer needs the server in user scope, because expansion is disabled for project-scoped files.
A shared server needs the value written literally; expansion resolves only in user-scoped configuration.
GITHUB_TOKEN is unset in that developer's shell, so the literal ${GITHUB_TOKEN} was passed through.
Expansion applies only to the args array, not the env block, so the file never expanded for anyone.

explanation: Expansion substitutes the value from the environment when the server starts. With no variable set and no default supplied, the placeholder is left as literal text and the server receives a token that is not a token.

why.A: Scope has no bearing on expansion, and moving the server would not set the missing variable.
why.B: Reverses the point of expansion, which exists so shared configuration can be committed without the value in it.
why.D: Expansion covers the env block along with commands, args, URLs and headers, and the rest of the team is working.

stem: You need every call site of a function named reconcileBalance across an unfamiliar 400-file repository. Which built-in tool fits?

options.text: Glob, since you are locating the files that contain the function.
Read on each file the module imports, following the chain to the call sites.
Bash with find piped to xargs, so you control the flags and the output format.
Grep, since you are searching file contents for an identifier.

explanation: Grep searches file contents, which is where identifiers, error messages and import statements live. One call returns every match with its location.

why.A: Glob matches file paths by name and extension; it cannot see what is inside a file.
why.B: Reads whole files to find a string that one content search returns directly, and misses callers outside the import chain.
why.C: Shells out to reimplement the built-in content search with no capability the built-in lacks.

stem: React tests are colocated next to the components they cover, for example Button.test.tsx beside Button.tsx. You need every one of them so you can apply a convention. Which tool fits?

options.text: Glob with a path pattern such as **/*.test.tsx.
Grep for "describe(" across the repository and collect the matching paths.
Read the test runner's configuration to get the list of files it collects.
Bash with find and a name filter, so the traversal order can be controlled.

explanation: Glob matches file paths by pattern, which is exactly finding files by extension no matter which directory they sit in.

why.B: Content search misses test files that use a different helper and matches non-test files that happen to use that one.
why.C: Runner config holds patterns rather than a file list, and files it is not yet configured for are invisible.
why.D: Reimplements Glob in a shell, and traversal order is not what the task turns on.

stem: Edit keeps failing on a 900-line generated API client: the anchor "return null;" appears eleven times, and each occurrence sits inside an identical three-line case block, so widening the anchor does not make it unique. What is the reliable fallback?

options.text: Split the change into eleven Edit calls, one for each occurrence in order.
Read the whole file, then Write it back with the modification applied.
Widen the anchor further until Edit resolves to exactly one occurrence.
Use Bash with sed to substitute the first occurrence of the anchor in place.

explanation: Edit depends on unique anchor text. When the file cannot supply one, reading the full contents and writing them back is the modification path that does not depend on matching.

why.A: Each of those calls hits the same non-unique anchor, so none of them can resolve.
why.C: The stem rules this out: the surrounding lines are identical too, so no wider anchor is unique either.
why.D: A shell substitution on an ambiguous pattern picks an occurrence by position rather than by intent.

stem: You are asked to understand how a 400-file payments service handles refunds, and you have no map of the codebase. What is the recommended exploration strategy?

options.text: Glob for all source files, then Read them in the order the package manifest lists them.
Ask the model to describe how refund flows are usually built in services of this shape.
Grep for the refund entry points, then Read those files and follow their imports.
Read every file in the service directory so nothing is missed, then reason over the whole.

explanation: Build understanding incrementally: a content search finds the entry points, and reading those files and their imports traces the actual flow without loading the codebase.

why.A: Still reads everything; manifest order is not call order and does not reduce what gets loaded.
why.B: Produces generic patterns instead of facts about this service, which is how plausible but wrong answers get written.
why.D: Exhausts the context window before any understanding starts, and most of those files are irrelevant.

stem: A utility is re-exported through three wrapper modules under different names, and call sites import whichever alias is local to them. You need every real usage. What is the reliable approach?

options.text: Grep the original function name only, since re-exports resolve back to it at build time.
Glob for files that import the original module's path, then read each of those files.
Read the three wrapper modules and treat the names in their import lists as the usages.
List every exported name across the wrappers first, then search for each name in turn.

explanation: Call sites reference the alias they imported, not the original name, so the search has to run once per exported name. Enumerating the names first is what makes the search complete.

why.A: Misses every call site written against an alias, which is most of them here.
why.B: Finds importers of one path and misses anything reached through a re-export chain.
why.C: The wrappers show what is re-exported, not who calls it, which is the question being asked.
